source.title: Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples
source.version: arXiv:2011.12940v2, posted 19 June 2021, 96 pages, the author's revision whose comment reads 'Changed title, rewrote introduction, improved results and exposition'; v1 is from 25 November 2020. The published version, Annals of Mathematics 199 (2024), no. 1, is behind the journal's paywall and was not consulted, so every locator gives the section, theorem or equation number together with the page of the arXiv v2 PDF, and the findings under sourceIssues are recorded against that version. No erratum or corrigendum is listed on the arXiv page or in Crossref.
readSections: §1 Introduction, pp. 2–13: §1.1 the main congruence and its combinatorial form, §1.2 the applications to Markoff triples and to connectedness of Hurwitz stacks, §1.3 the summary and sketch of the argument, §1.4 further directions, §1.6 notation

§2 Admissible G-covers of elliptic curves, pp. 13–33: §2.1 admissible G-covers and Adm(G)‾, §2.2 the reduced ramification divisor, §2.3 the Higman invariant, §2.4 stable marked G-curves, §2.5 G-structures, M(G), rigidification and the Galois dictionary

§3 Degrees of components of Adm(G)‾ over M(1)‾, pp. 33–42: §3.1 differentials and dualizing sheaves on stacks, §3.2 the universal family, §3.3 restriction to a ramified section, §3.4 degrees of line bundles on 1-dimensional stacks and the Hodge bundle, §3.5 the main congruence

§4 Galois correspondence for cuspidal objects, pp. 42–65: §§4.1–4.3 cuspidal covers, tangential base points and π₁(P¹−{0,1,∞}), §§4.4–4.7 normalization, gluing, balance and connectedness, §4.8 the δ-invariant, §4.9 the [−1]-pullback, §4.10 automorphism groups and the combinatorial congruence, §4.11 the dihedral obstruction, §4.12 congruences for simple groups

§5 Applications to Markoff triples and the geometry of M(SL₂(F_q)), pp. 65–87: §5.1 the trace invariant, §5.2 the character variety, §5.3 automorphism groups, §5.4 congruences, §5.5 strong approximation for the Markoff equation, §5.6 the genus formula and noncongruence

§6 Appendix, pp. 86–93: §6.1 normalized coordinates for tame balanced actions, §6.2 the normalizer of SL_n(F_q), §6.3 images of absolutely irreducible representations, §6.4 étale local rings of Deligne–Mumford stacks
References, pp. 93–96, read in full to identify the inputs listed under prerequisites

Review REV-PAPER-CHEN-24 (Claude Code, cc-39fac3, 23 September 2026): arXiv v2 (the same PDF, SHA-256 f60283b0…) and its TeX source read in full again; every item checked against it, and the claims of §5 recomputed over F_p. The published version (Ann. of Math. 199 (2024), 301–443) is paywalled and was not available to the review either. McCullough–Wanderley (Glasgow Math. J. 55 (2013), 481–509) was read for Conjecture 1.1.4.

summary: Complete extraction of the 96-page paper. Chen proves a congruence on the degree over the j-line of any connected component of the stack Adm(G)‾ of admissible G-covers of 1-generalized elliptic curves: with e the ramification index above the origin and d_X, m_X the two obstructions coming from the reduced ramification divisor and from the stackiness of degrees, deg(X → M(1)‾) ≡ 0 mod 12e/gcd(12e, m_X d_X). Through Galois theory this is a divisibility theorem for the cardinalities of Out⁺(Π)-orbits on Epi^ext(Π,G), that is for Nielsen equivalence classes of generating pairs. The proof rests on the isomorphism σ_O*ω_{E/X} ≅ (σ*ω_{C/X})^{⊗e}, on the Hodge bundle having degree 1/24, and on a combinatorial classification of the cusps of Adm(G)‾ by ℤ-orbits of conjugacy classes of generating pairs, the δ-invariant, which computes their automorphism groups. Applied to G = SL₂(F_p) with Higman invariant of trace −2 it gives that every Γ-orbit on the nonzero F_p-points of the Markoff surface has cardinality divisible by p; combined with Bourgain, Gamburd and Sarnak's estimates this makes their exceptional set finite and explicitly bounded, proves strong approximation for the Markoff equation outside it, and gives an exact genus formula for the resulting noncongruence modular curves. After the review, of the 123 items 5 are in the pinned libraries, 14 are planned by existing layers of the atlas and 104 are missing. The Markoff carrier goes to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4, which the accepted extractions of PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22 already make its owner; the Markoff-modulo-p endpoints go to the pending Part II of Arithmetic dynamics, the third paper to point there; Nielsen equivalence, T-systems and the two standing conjectures about them go to InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups IG.3 and IG.5; the general stack technology goes to AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry R09.4–R09.6; tangential base points go to AnabelianGeometryAndNonabelianChabauty NC.0; and the (g,n) = (1,1) Hurwitz theory itself, with its SL₂(F_q) consequences, forms a new roadmap, Nonabelian level structures on elliptic curves and congruences for Hurwitz components. 38 mistakes in the source are recorded, most found by the review, including a reversed condition in Theorem 1.1.2 and a gap in Lemma 4.12.2 for j ≥ 1; the arithmetic consequences of §5 were checked by exhaustive computation for p ≤ 23, including the orbit counts, the cusp count, the ramification above j = 0 and j = 1728 and the genus formula, which is correct. This is a paper inventory and routing, not a proof blueprint: the inputs quoted from Abramovich–Corti–Vistoli, Bertin–Romagny, Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, Macbeath, Nakamoto, Vdovin and Meiri–Puder are recorded as items with their own prerequisite entries and are not decomposed here.

items.name: Hurwitz stacks of covers of pointed curves
items.statement: For a field k, M_{g,n} is the moduli stack of smooth genus-g curves with n marked points, and for d ∈ ℤ the Hurwitz stack H_{g,n,d} classifies connected degree-d covers of smooth (g,n)-curves ramified only above the n marked points. The stacks M_{g,n} are irreducible while the H_{g,n,d} are typically disconnected, and the problem is to find combinatorial invariants of covers that separate their connected components.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1, p. 2, opening paragraph
items.note: IG.5 plans Hurwitz moduli with braid/Nielsen-class components; its reviewed audit records that no Hurwitz space or Nielsen class exists in either library. This paper works throughout with (g,n) = (1,1) and with G-Galois covers.

items.name: The moduli stack of elliptic curves and its compactification
items.statement: M(1) := M_{1,1} is the moduli stack of elliptic curves and M(1)‾ its compactification by stable 1-pointed curves of genus 1 (1-generalized elliptic curves); their coarse schemes are M(1) ≅ A¹_S and M(1)‾ ≅ P¹_S through the j-invariant.
items.note: R13.1 plans generalised elliptic curves and the Katz–Mazur layer plans the moduli formalism and its coarse schemes; the j-invariant of a Weierstrass curve is Mathlib's WeierstrassCurve.j. The stack M(1) itself, its compactification and the identification of the coarse space with the j-line are not in either library.

items.name: Congruence for the degree of a component of Adm(G) (Theorem 1.1.1)
items.statement: Work over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0 (e.g. ℚ‾). Let G be a finite group, c ∈ G with conjugacy class 𝔠, and let X ⊂ Adm(G)‾_𝔠 be a connected component with coarse scheme X, parametrising covers with Higman invariant 𝔠. For a prime ℓ put r := ord_ℓ(|c|). (a) Write ord_ℓ(|G|) = r + s and let j ≥ 0 be an integer such that G has no proper normal subgroup of order divisible by ℓ^{j+1}. If r ≥ 3s + j then deg(X → M(1)‾) ≡ 0 mod ℓ^{⌈(r−3s−j)/2⌉}. (b) If G is nonabelian simple, ℓ^{r+1} ≥ |G|^{1/3} and G is not isomorphic to PSL₂(F_q) for any prime power q, then deg(X → M(1)‾) ≡ 0 mod ℓ^{⌈r/2⌉}.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.1, p. 4, Theorem 1.1.1; proved as Corollary 4.12.5
items.note: |c| is the ramification index at every ramified point, since the stabiliser of a ramified point is generated by a conjugate of c. Acceptance: for c = [[−1,1],[0,−1]] ∈ SL₂(F_ℓ) with ℓ ≥ 3 one has r = 1, s = j = 0 and the congruence is ≡ 0 mod ℓ, which is the Markoff case. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Omits the standing base: §1.1 (p. 4) and §1.3.2 (p. 9) work over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0, and Adm(G)‾_𝔠 is only defined over ℚ‾ (Definition 2.3.4, p. 20). Otherwise exact.

items.name: Combinatorial form of the congruence (Theorem 1.1.2)
items.statement: Let G be a finite group, c ∈ G with conjugacy class 𝔠, fix a basis (a,b) of the free group Π of rank 2 and let ϕ : Π ↠ G be a surjection with ϕ([a,b]) ∈ 𝔠; let Out⁺(Π)·ϕ be its orbit in Epi^ext(Π,G). For a prime ℓ put r := ord_ℓ(|c|). (a) Write ord_ℓ(|G|) = r + s and let j ≥ 0 be such that G has no proper normal subgroup of order divisible by ℓ^{j+1}; if r ≥ 3s + j then |Out⁺(Π)·ϕ| ≡ 0 mod ℓ^{⌈(r−3s−j)/2⌉}. (b) If G is nonabelian simple, ℓ^{r+1} ≥ |G|^{1/3} and G ≇ PSL₂(F_q) for every q, then |Out⁺(Π)·ϕ| ≡ 0 mod ℓ^{⌈r/2⌉}. Let γ_{−I} ∈ Aut(Π) be (a,b) ↦ (a^{−1},b^{−1}). If ϕ∘γ_{−I} ≠ ϕ in Epi^ext(Π,G) (i.e. ϕ∘γ_{−I} is not Inn(G)-conjugate to ϕ), then |Out⁺(Π)·ϕ| = 2·deg(X → M(1)‾) for the corresponding component X, and the congruences mod ℓ^k strengthen to mod 2ℓ^k. (Equivalently, as in Corollary 4.12.5, every Out⁺(Π)-orbit on Epi^ext(Π,G)_𝔠/⟨γ_{−I}⟩ has cardinality divisible by the same powers of ℓ.)
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.1, p. 5, Theorem 1.1.2; deduced from Corollary 4.12.5 via Theorem 2.5.2(4)
items.note: Acceptance: for G = ℤ/nℤ the action is transitive with single orbit of size [SL₂(ℤ):Γ₁(n)]; for G = (ℤ/nℤ)² there are φ(n) orbits each of size [SL₂(ℤ):Γ(n)] = |SL₂(ℤ/nℤ)|, so the congruences are vacuous for abelian G. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: The final sentence copies a reversed condition from the paper (see the new issue on Theorem 1.1.2). The coarse degree of the component equals |O/⟨γ_{−I}⟩| for the orbit O = Out⁺(Π)·ϕ (Theorem 2.5.2(4)). Because γ_{−I} is central in Out⁺(Π), it either fixes O pointwise, which happens exactly when ϕ∘γ_{−I} = ϕ in Epi^ext, or acts on O freely. So the factor 2 is gained exactly when ϕ∘γ_{−I} ≠ ϕ in Epi^ext(Π,G). Counterexample to the printed version: G = ℤ/2ℤ, c = 1, any odd ℓ. Then r = s = j = 0 and ϕ∘γ_{−I} = −ϕ = ϕ, but the only orbit has 3 elements, and 3 ≢ 0 mod 2. Also, the theorem is entirely on p. 5.

items.name: Exterior epimorphisms, Nielsen equivalence classes and T-systems
items.statement: For groups A, B, Epi^ext(A,B) := Epi(A,B)/Inn(B) is the set of conjugacy classes of surjections A → B. Having fixed a basis of the free group F_r, Epi^ext(F_r,G) is the set of conjugacy classes of generating r-tuples of G, the Out(F_r)-orbits on it are the Nielsen equivalence classes of generating tuples, and the orbits on Epi(F_r,G)/Aut(G) are the T_r-systems. d(G) denotes the least cardinality of a generating set of G.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1, p. 3, (1); §1.1, p. 5 (Nielsen equivalence, T_r-systems, d(G)); §1.6, p. 12
items.note: Nielsen equivalence of generating tuples is not in either library: Mathlib's NielsenSchreier is the unrelated theorem that subgroups of free groups are free. API: the Out(F_r)-action on Epi^ext, the quotient by Aut(G), and the count of orbits. Tests: for G = ℤ/nℤ and r = 2 there is one class; for G = (ℤ/nℤ)² there are φ(n). Review note on status: Partly in the direction of InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5 (Hurwitz moduli with braid/Nielsen-class components), but no stage defines Nielsen classes of generating r-tuples of an arbitrary finite group or T_r-systems; 'missing' is reasonable.

items.name: Wiegold–Garion transitivity conjecture (Conjecture 1.1.3)
items.statement: If G is a finite group and r ≥ d(G) + 1, then Out(F_r) acts transitively on Epi^ext(F_r,G).
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.1, p. 5, Conjecture 1.1.3, quoting [Gar08, Conjecture 1]
items.note: A conjecture, known for solvable G [Dun70] and for r ≥ log₂|G| [Lub11]; it must never be consumed as a theorem. For finite simple G it is attributed to Wiegold.

items.name: The trace invariant and the T-classification conjecture (Conjecture 1.1.4)
items.statement: For G = SL₂(F_q) the trace invariant is τ : Epi(Π,SL₂(F_q)) → F_q, ϕ ↦ tr ϕ([a,b]); it is constant on Nielsen classes. Since Aut(SL₂(F_q)) is generated by GL₂(F_q)-conjugation and field automorphisms, the invariant of a T₂-system is the weak trace invariant, the Aut(F_q)-orbit of τ(ϕ). The T-classification conjecture of McCullough–Wanderley [MW13, §§1, 4] says: for non-exceptional q (q ∉ {3,5,7,9,11}), the weak trace invariant is a bijection from the set of T₂-systems of SL₂(F_q) onto the set of Aut(F_q)-orbits in F_q other than {2}. For q = p a prime ≥ 13 this says that τ induces a bijection from the T₂-systems of SL₂(F_p) onto F_p − {2}; this is the form in the paper, with 'its image' for F_p − {2}. MW13 verify their stronger Classification Conjecture, which implies it, by computer for all q ≤ 101.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.1, p. 5, Conjecture 1.1.4, quoting [MW13]
items.note: A conjecture. The case (q,t) = (p,−2) is resolved for all but finitely many p by Theorem 1.2.6. It contains the Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak conjecture as the special case (q,t) = (p,−2). Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: This misstates [MW13] (the paper's own error, see the new issue on Conjecture 1.1.4). For q = p^f with f > 1, Aut(SL₂(F_q)) contains field automorphisms, and these change tr ϕ([a,b]). So τ is not constant on T₂-systems, and MW13 conjecture a bijection for the weak trace invariant, the Aut(F_q)-orbit of τ. MW13 also exclude the exceptional q ∈ {3,5,7,9,11}. The published MW13 (Glasgow Math. J. 55 (2013)) reports computer verification for q ≤ 101, not q ≤ 131.

items.name: Trace coordinates classify SL₂(F_q)-representations of the free group of rank two
items.statement: For a prime power q and t ∈ F_q − {2}, the map Hom(Π,SL₂(F_q))_t / GL₂(F_q) → {(x,y,z) ∈ F_q³ : x²+y²+z²−xyz−2 = t}, ϕ ↦ (tr ϕ(a), tr ϕ(b), tr ϕ(ab)), is a bijection, where GL₂(F_q) acts by conjugation and Hom(Π,SL₂(F_q))_t is the set of ϕ with tr ϕ([a,b]) = t. The natural Aut(Π)-action on the source induces an action on the target by polynomial automorphisms of A³ preserving the hypersurface, and the induced group Γ ⊂ Aut(A³) is generated by the coordinate permutations and the Vieta involution (x,y,z) ↦ (x,y,xy−z).
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.2, pp. 5–6, (2); proved as Theorem 5.2.10 with Proposition 5.2.5
items.note: This is the dictionary between the moduli stacks M(G) for G ≤ SL₂(F_q) and the Γ-action on F_q-points of the level sets of x²+y²+z²−xyz−2. Acceptance: the fibre over t = −2 is the Markoff surface.

items.name: The Markoff surface in trace coordinates and its nonzero points
items.statement: X ⊂ A³_ℤ is the affine surface x² + y² + z² − xyz = 0 and, for a prime p, X*(p) := X(F_p) − {(0,0,0)}. For odd p the bijection above restricts to a bijection Epi(Π,SL₂(F_p))_{−2}/GL₂(F_p) ≅ X*(p).
items.note: X is the twist by (x,y,z) ↦ (3x,3y,3z) of the classical Markoff surface M : x²+y²+z²−3xyz = 0; the twist is an isomorphism over ℤ[1/3] and a bijection on ℤ-points. The same carrier is routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 by the accepted extractions of PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22 and must not be planned twice.

items.name: Markoff's theorem on positive integral solutions (Theorem 1.2.1)
items.statement: The positive integer solutions of x²+y²+z²−xyz = 0 form a single orbit under Γ.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.2.1, p. 6, Theorem 1.2.1, quoting [Mar79, Mar80]
items.note: The same statement is item /3 of the accepted extraction PAPER-MARTIN-25 in the coefficient-three normalisation; the two must share one carrier. Acceptance: the orbit of (3,3,3) in the coefficient-one normalisation.

items.name: The Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak conjecture (Conjecture 1.2.2)
items.statement: For every prime p, Γ acts transitively on X*(p); equivalently X(F_p) is the union of at most the two orbits {(0,0,0)} and X*(p), and X*(p) is empty exactly for p = 3.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.2.1, p. 6, Conjecture 1.2.2; restated as Conjecture 5.5.1, p. 81
items.note: First posed by Baragar in 1991. A positive answer implies that X(ℤ) → X(F_p) is surjective for every p, that is strong approximation for the Markoff equation. This paper proves it for all p outside an explicitly bounded finite set.

items.name: The Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak theorems (Theorems 1.2.3 and 1.2.4)
items.statement: Let E_bgs be the set of primes for which Γ does not act transitively on X*(p). (a) For every ε > 0, #{p ∈ E_bgs : p ≤ x} = O(x^ε). (b) If C(p) is the largest Γ-orbit on X*(p) then |X*(p) − C(p)| ≤ p^ε for all large p. Equivalently, in group-theoretic form, the same two statements hold for the Out(Π)-action on Epi(Π,SL₂(F_p))_{−2}/GL₂(F_p).
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.2.1, pp. 6–7, Theorems 1.2.3 and 1.2.4; restated as Theorems 5.5.2 and 5.5.3
items.note: Quoted from [BGS16a]; this paper does not reprove them. Their methods are effective, which is what makes the exceptional set explicitly bounded. Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak is listed under prerequisites and is shared with the pending Part II of Arithmetic dynamics.

items.name: Every orbit on X*(p) has size divisible by p (Theorem 1.2.5)
items.statement: For every prime p ≥ 3, every Out⁺(Π)-orbit on Epi(Π,SL₂(F_p))_{−2}/GL₂(F_p) has cardinality divisible by p; equivalently every Γ-orbit on X*(p) has cardinality divisible by p.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.2.1, p. 7, Theorem 1.2.5; proved as Theorem 5.5.4
items.note: Immediate from Theorem 1.1.2(a) once one knows that ϕ([a,b]) is conjugate to [[−1,u],[0,−1]] with u ∈ F_p^×, hence of order 2p, so that r = ord_p(2p) = 1 and s = j = 0. Acceptance: |X*(p)| = p(p±3) is divisible by p.

items.name: Finiteness of the exceptional set and strong approximation (Theorem 1.2.6)
items.statement: (a) The exceptional set E_bgs is finite and explicitly bounded. (b) For every prime p ∉ E_bgs the Markoff surface X satisfies strong approximation at p, that is X(ℤ) → X(F_p) is surjective.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.2.1, p. 7, Theorem 1.2.6; proved as Theorems 5.5.5 and 5.5.7
items.note: Combines Theorem 1.2.5 (every orbit has size ≥ p) with Theorem 1.2.3(b) (the complement of the largest orbit has size ≤ p^ε). A preliminary explicit bound of approximately 10^{5547000} for the largest prime in E_bgs was obtained by Elena Fuchs; the conjecture is verified for all p < 3000 by de Courcy-Ireland and Lee, so the conjecture is reduced to a finite computation.

items.name: Congruences for generalized Markoff equations (Theorem 1.2.7)
items.statement: Let q ≥ 3 be a prime power and t ∈ F_q − {2,−2}, written t = ω + ω^{−1} with ω ∈ F_{q²}^× − {±1} and {ω,ω^{−1}} uniquely determined by t. Let P = (A,B,C) be an F_q-point of x²+y²+z²−xyz = t+2 with at least two of A, B, C nonzero, and let Γ act by the same formulas as on X. Let ℓ be an odd prime, r := ord_ℓ(|ω|) and write ord_ℓ(|SL₂(F_q)|) = ord_ℓ(q³−q) = r + s. Then the Γ-orbit of P has cardinality ≡ 0 mod ℓ^{max{r−s,0}}.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.2.1, p. 7, Theorem 1.2.7; proved as Theorems 5.4.4 and 5.5.9
items.note: The case t = −2 is the Markoff equation; t = 2 is the Cayley cubic, where the methods give nothing new because its F_q-points correspond to representations with image in a Borel subgroup.

items.name: Connectedness of the Hurwitz stacks Adm(SL₂(F_p))_{c} and the genus formula (Theorem 1.2.9)
items.statement: Let p ≥ 5 be a prime not in E_bgs, and 𝔠₁, 𝔠₂ the two noncentral conjugacy classes of SL₂(F_p) of trace −2, represented by [[−1,1],[0,−1]] and [[−1,a],[0,−1]] with a a non-square. The stacks Adm(SL₂(F_p))‾_{𝔠ᵢ} over ℚ‾, i = 1, 2, are isomorphic and connected; let M_p‾ be the coarse scheme of either. With Φ(n) := Σ_{d|n} φ(d)/d, genus(M_p‾) = p²/12 − ((p−1)/4)Φ(p−1) − ((p+1)/4)Φ(p+1) + ε(p), where ε(p) = 7p/8 − 29/24, 5p/8 + 19/24, 7p/8 − 17/24 or 5p/8 + 7/24 according as p ≡ 1, 3, 5 or 7 mod 8. For p ≥ 13 the genus is ≥ 2, and for p = 5, 7, 11 it is 0, 0, 1. Consequently, by Faltings' theorem, for p ≥ 13, p ∉ E_bgs, and any number field K, only finitely many elliptic curves over K admit an SL₂(F_p)-cover branched only over the origin with ramification index 2p.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.2.2, p. 8, Theorem 1.2.9; proved as Theorems 5.6.3 and 5.6.4
items.note: Interpretable as an analogue of Rademacher's conjecture for the noncongruence modular curves M_p. Acceptance: genus 0, 0, 1 at p = 5, 7, 11 and the asymptotic p²/12. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: 'odd prime' should be 'p ≥ 5'. For p = 3, −2 ≡ 1 is not a 3-admissible trace (Proposition 5.1.3(a)) and X*(3) = ∅, so the stacks Adm(SL₂(F₃))_{𝔠ᵢ} are empty, not connected. The paper counts 3 ∉ E_bgs (§5.5, p. 81: the action on X*(3) = ∅ is called transitive), so the printed hypothesis admits p = 3. The source is Theorem 5.6.3, which assumes p ≥ 5 (see the new issue). ε(p) should be stated explicitly: 'ε(p) ∼ p' is loose, since ε(p) ≈ 7p/8 or 5p/8.

items.name: The main congruence in its purest form (Theorem 1.3.1)
items.statement: Work over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0. Let X ⊂ Adm(G)‾ be a connected component classifying G-covers of elliptic curves with ramification index e ≥ 2 above the origin. Let R be a connected component of the reduced ramification divisor of the universal family C → E → X, with coarse scheme R, so that C_R → R has a ramified section σ. Let d_X be the degree of the induced map of coarse schemes R → X. Let m_X be the least positive integer such that (σ*Ω_{C_R/R})^{⊗m_X} has trivial local characters. Then the map of coarse schemes f : X → M(1)‾ satisfies deg(f) ≡ 0 mod 12e/gcd(12e, m_X d_X).
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §1.3.2, p. 10, Theorem 1.3.1; proved as Theorem 3.5.1
items.note: The prototype is: σ_O*Ω_{E/X} ≅ (σ*Ω_{C/X})^{⊗e} and σ_O*Ω_{E/X} = f*λ with λ the Hodge bundle of degree 1/24, so deg f · deg λ = e · deg(σ*Ω_{C/X}) and integrality of degrees forces the congruence. The two obstructions are that the universal cover need not admit a ramified section (giving d_X) and that degrees on a stack are only rational (giving m_X). Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Omits the standing base: §1.1 (p. 4) and §1.3.2 (p. 9) work over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0, and Adm(G)‾_𝔠 is only defined over ℚ‾ (Definition 2.3.4, p. 20). Also, d_X and m_X require a component R of the reduced ramification divisor, which exists only when e ≥ 2.

items.name: Question 1.4.1 on nonabelian simple groups
items.statement: If G is a nonabelian simple group, must every component X ⊂ Adm(G)‾ classifying covers with ramification index e satisfy deg(X → M(1)‾) ≡ 0 mod e? Combinatorially: if ϕ : Π ↠ G is a surjection with ϕ([a,b]) of order e, must the Out⁺(Π)-orbit of ϕ in Epi^ext(Π,G) have cardinality divisible by e?
items.note: Open. Verified computationally for every nonabelian finite simple group of order ≤ 29120, a total of 352 non-isomorphic connected components, including PSL₂(F_q) for q = 5,…,37, A₅,…,A₈, M₁₁, PSL₃(F₃), PSL₃(F₄), PSU₃(F₃), O₅(F₃) and Sz(8). It must be recorded as a question, never as a theorem.

items.name: Nodal, prestable and stable pointed curves
items.statement: A morphism f : C → S is a nodal curve if it is flat, proper, of finite presentation with geometric fibres of pure dimension 1 whose only singularities are ordinary double points, and a prestable curve if moreover the geometric fibres are connected. A prestable n-pointed curve of genus g is a prestable curve with n disjoint sections in the smooth locus whose geometric fibres have arithmetic genus g; it is stable if every geometric fibre has finitely many automorphisms fixing the sections, equivalently every genus-0 component of a normalised fibre carries at least three special points and every genus-1 component at least one, equivalently ω_{C_s}(Σσ_i) is ample.
items.note: Layer 3 of the Tau Ceti roadmap Stable reduction of curves and stable maps plans prestable, semistable, stable and pointed curves; that roadmap is existing work and is never re-planned here. This paper additionally uses the generic locus C_gen, the complement of the special points.

items.name: 1-generalized elliptic curves
items.statement: A 1-generalized elliptic curve is a stable 1-pointed curve of genus 1, with section σ_O and divisor O; the moduli stack of such is M(1)‾ and the open substack of smooth ones is M(1). Up to isomorphism there is exactly one nodal (non-smooth) 1-generalized elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field.
items.note: R13.1 plans generalised elliptic curves, n-gons, contraction and the group law on the smooth locus. Chen's 1-generalized elliptic curves are the stable-pointed rather than the Deligne–Rapoport formulation, and the comparison (Remark 4.10.4, recovering [DR75, Theorem 2.7]) is part of this paper.

items.name: Admissible G-covers of prestable pointed curves
items.statement: Let S be a scheme (in the paper a ℤ[1/|G|]-scheme). An admissible G-cover of a prestable n-pointed curve (D → S, {σ_i}) is a finite map π : C → D with a right G-action on C leaving π invariant, such that: (1) C → S is a prestable curve; (2) every node of C maps to a node of D; (3) over D_gen, π is a G-torsor; (4) at a geometric point p̄ of C over a marking, with image s̄ in S, there is e ≥ 1 such that the strict localisations of C → D → S at p̄ are isomorphic over S_(s̄) to those of Spec O_{S,s̄}[ξ] → Spec O_{S,s̄}[x], x ↦ ξ^e, at ξ = 0; (5) at a geometric point p̄ of C over a node, with image s̄, there are r ≥ 1 and a ∈ m_{S,s̄} such that the strict localisations are isomorphic to those of Spec O_{S,s̄}[ξ,η]/(ξη−a) → Spec O_{S,s̄}[x,y]/(xy−a^r), (x,y) ↦ (ξ^r,η^r), at (0,0); (6) at every geometric point p̄ of C lying over a node, in the notation of (5) applied to the fibre C_s̄, the stabiliser G_p̄ is cyclic, of order r, and a generator acts étale-locally by ξ ↦ ζξ, η ↦ ζ^{−1}η for some primitive r-th root of unity ζ ∈ k(s̄) (the node is balanced). It is smooth if C/S is smooth.
items.note: Following [ACV03, §4]; Chen requires C prestable, so ACV-admissible covers are the same conditions (2)–(6) without connected fibres. API: the six conditions as predicates, base change, the local models, and the smooth locus. Tests: a G-torsor over a smooth elliptic curve minus the origin extends to an admissible G-cover ramified only there; an unbalanced node action is excluded because it forces a = 0. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Condition (6) repeats the paper's misprint 'primitive e-th root of unity' (see the new issue on Definition 2.1.4(6)). At a node the stabiliser G_p̄ has order r, the integer of (5), and a generator acts through a primitive r-th root of unity. The e of (4) is the ramification index over the markings, which in general differs from r.

items.name: Elementary properties of admissible G-covers (Remark 2.1.5)
items.statement: (a) Condition (2) follows from (3) and (4); admissible G-covers send smooth points to smooth points, so x ∈ C is a node exactly when π(x) is, and C/S is smooth exactly when D/S is. (b) An admissible G-cover is an ACV-admissible G-cover with connected geometric fibres. (c) A finite map satisfying (1)–(5) is an admissible cover, and a G-action satisfying (6) is balanced; an unbalanced node cannot appear in a generically smooth family. (d) Balancedness at a node is equivalent to: the normalisation splits the cotangent space at the node into two lines, the action of G_p preserves that splitting and acts faithfully by mutually inverse characters.
items.note: Part (d) is proved in the appendix as Proposition 6.1.4. Tests: the two branches of a node and the mutually inverse characters; an action with ζ' ≠ ζ^{−1} forces a = 0.

items.name: The stacks Adm(G)‾, Adm⁰(G) and their morphisms
items.statement: A morphism of admissible G-covers is a cartesian G-equivariant diagram compatible with the sections; it is determined by the map C' → C. The category Adm‾_{g,n}(G) of ACV-admissible G-covers of stable n-pointed genus-g curves is fibred in groupoids over Sch/S, the admissible ones form an open and closed substack, and one writes Adm(G)‾ := Adm‾^{conn}_{1,1}(G) with Adm⁰(G) ⊂ Adm(G)‾ the open substack of smooth covers, so Adm⁰(G) = φ^{−1}(M(1)) for the forgetful functor φ. A morphism of admissible G-covers need not induce the identity on the base curve.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.1, p. 15, Definition 2.1.6 and Remark 2.1.7 (Definition 2.1.8 is the coarse-space definition, which belongs to item 24)
items.note: API: the fibred category, its open and closed decomposition, the forgetful functor to M(1)‾, and the coarse schemes Adm(G)‾, Adm⁰(G). Tests: two admissible G-covers of the same curve can be isomorphic through an automorphism of the base.

items.name: Coarse spaces and the Keel–Mori theorem (Theorem 2.1.9)
items.statement: A coarse space of an algebraic stack X is a map c : X → X to an algebraic space that is initial among maps to algebraic spaces and induces a bijection X(k)/≅ → X(k) for every algebraically closed field k. If X is locally of finite presentation over S with finite inertia (e.g. separated, locally finitely presented and Deligne–Mumford), the coarse space exists and: (a) c is proper, quasi-finite and a universal homeomorphism; (b) its formation commutes with flat base change; (c) c_*O_X = O_X; (d) if X is separated over S so is X; (e) if S is locally Noetherian, X is locally of finite presentation over S; (f) if S is locally Noetherian and X is proper over S, X is proper over S.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.1, pp. 15–16, Definition 2.1.8 and Theorem 2.1.9
items.note: R09.5 plans the existence of coarse spaces for finite-inertia presentations and their base-change statements; its reviewed audit records that neither library has coarse moduli spaces or the Keel–Mori theorem. Chen uses (a)–(f) throughout without further comment. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: (e) and (f) need the hypothesis that the base S is locally Noetherian (Theorem 2.1.9(e),(f)); the item states them without it.

items.name: Smoothness of the coarse scheme of a 1-dimensional stack (Lemma 2.1.10)
items.statement: Let X be a smooth proper Deligne–Mumford stack over a regular Noetherian scheme S whose fibres have pure dimension 1, and suppose its coarse space X is a scheme. Then X is smooth and proper over S.
items.note: Proof route: the local structure of Deligne–Mumford stacks gives an étale cover by [V_i/G_i] with V_i smooth affine, and quotients of smooth affine curves by finite groups are smooth by [KM85, p. 508]. Tests: the j-line as the coarse space of M(1).

items.name: Adm(G)‾ is a smooth proper Deligne–Mumford stack (Theorem 2.1.11)
items.statement: Over S = Spec ℤ[1/|G|]: (a) Adm(G)‾ is a smooth proper Deligne–Mumford stack of pure dimension 1 over S, with finite diagonal; (b) the forgetful map φ : Adm(G)‾ → M(1)‾, (C → E → S) ↦ (E → S), is flat, proper and quasi-finite, and Adm⁰(G) ⊂ Adm(G)‾ is open and dense; (c) Adm(G)‾ has a coarse scheme Adm(G)‾ with the properties of Theorem 2.1.9, and the induced map Adm(G)‾ → M(1)‾ is finite; in particular Adm(G)‾ is a scheme.
items.note: Quoted from Abramovich–Vistoli and Abramovich–Corti–Vistoli through the equivalence of Adm‾_{1,1}(G) with the stack of twisted G-covers. Properness is what makes the main congruence work; the map φ is not finite, which is why M(G)‾ is introduced. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: 'over S' should name the base, S = Spec ℤ[1/|G|] (§2, p. 13). Smoothness and the finiteness claims use that |G| is invertible.

items.name: Fixed loci and the reduced ramification divisor (Lemma 2.2.1, Proposition 2.2.2, Definition 2.2.3)
items.statement: (Lemma 2.2.1) If C → S is smooth, two closed subschemes of C that are finite étale over S and have the same support are equal. (Proposition 2.2.2) Let S be a ℤ[1/|G|]-scheme and π : C → D an admissible G-cover of a stable n-pointed curve D over S. For a nontrivial cyclic H ≤ G let C^H := ∩_{h∈H} C^h, the scheme-theoretic intersection of the equalisers of id and h (equal to C^h for a generator h). Then C^H_sm := C^H ∩ C_sm = (C_sm)^H is either empty or an effective Cartier divisor in C finite étale over S, and its formation commutes with arbitrary base change. (Definition 2.2.3) Δ(H) := C^H_sm − ∪_{K ⊋ H cyclic} C^K_sm; its support is the set of x ∈ C_sm with Hx = x, H acting trivially on κ(x), and no strictly larger subgroup doing both. The reduced ramification divisor is R_π := ⊔_H Δ(H), over the nontrivial cyclic H ≤ G.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.2, pp. 17–18, Lemma 2.2.1, Proposition 2.2.2 and Definition 2.2.3, following [BR11]
items.note: The Δ(H) are pairwise disjoint. API: C^H, Δ(H), R_π, the G-action on R_π and base change. Tests: for a free action R_π is empty; over a marking with ramification index e the local picture is Spec A[t]/((ζ−1)t) ⊂ Spec A[t]. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: The divisor statement is about the source of an admissible G-cover of a stable n-pointed curve over a ℤ[1/|G|]-scheme S. The item puts this context only in the last clause, and without it the Cartier/étale claim is false: the proof uses that fixed points lie over markings and that ζ − 1 is a unit.

items.name: The reduced ramification divisor is finite étale (Propositions 2.2.4 and 2.2.6)
items.statement: Let S be a connected ℤ[1/|G|]-scheme, π : C → D an admissible G-cover of a stable n-pointed curve (D,σ₁,…,σₙ) over S, and e_i the ramification index above σ_i. Then R_π is an effective Cartier divisor, finite étale over S, supported on the non-étale points of C_sm → D_sm; if e_i ≥ 2, σ_i*R_π := R_π ×_{D,σ_i} S is finite étale over S of degree |G|/e_i. R_π is reduced iff S is reduced. The Riemann–Hurwitz ramification divisor 𝔑_π := Div(π*ω_{D/S} → ω_{C/S}), in the sense of Knudsen–Mumford, satisfies σ_i*𝔑_π = (e_i − 1)·σ_i*R_π.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.2, p. 18, Proposition 2.2.4 and Remark 2.2.5
items.note: Tests: degree |G|/e over the origin for a cover of an elliptic curve branched only there; the divisor is not reduced over a non-reduced base. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: The locator cites Proposition 2.2.6, but the statement omits it: the Galois groups of the components of R_π lie in N_G(G_x̄)/G_x̄, and in C_G(G_x̄)/G_x̄ when S is regular and integral with a primitive e-th root of unity. The coverage section proposes it as a separate item. Also, 'of which it is a factor' should be the exact relation σ_i*𝔑_π = (e_i − 1)·σ_i*R_π.

items.name: The Higman invariant of an admissible G-cover
items.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field, G a finite group with |G| ∈ k^×, (D,O) a 1-pointed prestable curve over k, and π : C → D an admissible G-cover with ramification index e over O. For x ∈ π^{−1}(O), G_x is cyclic of order e and acts faithfully on the cotangent line, giving χ_x : G_x ≅ μ_e(k), with χ_{xg} ∘ i_{g^{−1}} = χ_x. For a primitive n-th root of unity ζ_n ∈ k with e | n, the algebraic Higman invariant Hig_{ζ_n}(π) is the conjugacy class of χ_x^{−1}(ζ_n^{n/e}), independent of x. Over ℂ, with the monodromy representation φ_x : π₁^top(D_gen(ℂ),y) → G defined by γ·x = x·φ_x(γ), the topological Higman invariant, the class of φ_x(γ_O) for a small counter-clockwise loop γ_O around O, equals Hig_{exp(2πi/n)}(π); the paper asserts this and leaves the check to the reader. For an elliptic curve E/ℂ and a positively oriented basis a, b of π₁^top(E°(ℂ),x₀), φ_x is surjective and the Higman invariant is the class of φ_x([b,a]) = [φ_x(b),φ_x(a)]. So it is a commutator of a generating pair, and for abelian G every object of Adm(G)‾ has trivial Higman invariant.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.3, pp. 19–20, Definition 2.3.1 and Remark 2.3.3
items.note: Also called the Nielsen type. API: the invariant relative to a compatible system of roots of unity, its independence of the chosen point, and the commutator description. Tests: abelian G gives the trivial class, so abelian covers of elliptic curves unramified away from the origin are unramified everywhere. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Omits the setting: k is algebraically closed and |G| is invertible in k (needed for G_x cyclic and χ_x faithful). The comparison over ℂ holds for ζ_n = exp(2πi/n), and the paper leaves it to the reader (Remark 2.3.3).

items.name: Local constancy of the Higman invariant and the decomposition of Adm(G)‾ (Proposition 2.3.2, Definition 2.3.4)
items.statement: Let S be a ℤ[1/|G|]-scheme with a primitive n-th root of unity ζ_n ∈ Γ(S,O_S), where n is a multiple of every ramification index (e.g. n = |G|). Then the functions e : |Adm(G)‾| → ℕ and Hig_{ζ_n} : |Adm(G)‾| → Cl(G) are locally constant. For S = Spec ℚ‾ and Hig := Hig_{exp(2πi/|G|)}, this gives decompositions M(G)‾_ℚ‾ = ⊔_{𝔠∈Cl(G)} M(G)‾_𝔠 and Adm(G)‾_ℚ‾ = ⊔_𝔠 Adm(G)‾_𝔠 into open and closed substacks of fixed Higman invariant, with coarse schemes M(G)‾_𝔠 and Adm(G)‾_𝔠.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.3, pp. 20–21, Proposition 2.3.2 and Definition 2.3.4
items.note: Tests: the ramification index is the order of the Higman invariant; for SL₂(F_p) and trace −2 there are exactly two noncentral classes, giving two components. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Omits the hypothesis on the base. The paper assumes a primitive n-th root of unity ζ_n ∈ Γ(S,O_S), and Hig_{ζ_n}(ξ) is defined only when e(ξ) | n, e.g. n = |G|.

items.name: Quotients of curves by finite group actions (Lemma 2.4.1)
items.statement: Let C → S be flat, proper and finitely presented with reduced geometric fibres of pure dimension 1, and let a finite group G act S-linearly on C. Then (a) C is a union of G-invariant affine opens; (b) the categorical quotient C/G exists, π : C → C/G is finite and O_{C/G} ≅ (π_*O_C)^G; (c) if |G| is invertible on S, formation of C/G commutes with arbitrary base change. (a) and (b) need no tameness hypothesis.
items.note: Tests: the quotient of a nodal curve by a balanced action is again nodal; base change along S' → S. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Part (c) needs |G| invertible on S (the paper's standing tameness hypothesis, via [KM85, A7.1.3(4)]); the item implies this but should state it. The paper's proof of (a) has a gap (see the new issue on Lemma 2.4.1).

items.name: Stable marked G-curves
items.statement: A marking on a prestable curve C → S is an effective Cartier divisor R ⊂ C étale over S, necessarily inside the smooth locus and finite étale over S; a marked prestable curve is a pair (C/S,R), and it is stable if its geometric fibres have finite automorphism groups preserving R. A stable marked G-curve is a stable marked curve with a faithful right G-action such that (a) R is preserved, (b) C → C/G is étale on C_sm − R, and (c) the action at every geometric node is balanced.
items.note: This is the curve-with-action point of view: one forgets the base curve and remembers C, its G-action and the marking. Tests: an elliptic curve with trivial marking and trivial action; a hyperelliptic curve with its involution and Weierstrass points.

items.name: Admissible G-covers are the same as stable marked G-curves (Propositions 2.4.4, 2.4.6, 2.4.8 and Theorem 2.4.9)
items.statement: For a stable marked G-curve (C/S,R) the quotient (C/G, R/G) is a stable marked curve and C → C/G is finite flat. For an admissible G-cover π of an n-pointed stable curve, with associated marking R := ⊔R_i where R_i is Z_i := C ×_{D,σ_i} S when R_π misses it and R_π ×_{D,σ_i} S otherwise, the pair (C/S,R) is a stable marked G-curve, the quotient C/G exists, commutes with base change and π induces an isomorphism C/G ≅ D. Conversely, objects of the category H‾_{g,n,G} of stable marked G-curves with a decomposition R = ⊔R_i such that G preserves each R_i, each R_i/G → S is an isomorphism and C/G is a prestable curve of genus g, give admissible G-covers, and the functor Φ is an equivalence H‾_{g,n,G} ≅ Adm‾^{conn}_{g,n}(G). In particular H‾_G := H‾_{1,1,G} is a smooth proper Deligne–Mumford stack of pure dimension 1 over S.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.4, pp. 22–23, Propositions 2.4.4, 2.4.6, 2.4.8, Definitions 2.4.5, 2.4.7 and Theorem 2.4.9
items.note: This equivalence is what makes the deformation theory of Proposition 2.5.3 available. Tests: the marking of a cover with ramification index 1 above a marking is the whole preimage; the quotient map recovers the base curve.

items.name: G-structures on elliptic curves and the stack M(G)
items.statement: For a finite group G, T_G is the sheafification, for the topology on M(1) induced by the étale topology, of the presheaf E/S ↦ {G-torsors X → E° := E − O with geometrically connected fibres over S}/≅. A G-structure on E/S is a section of T_G, and M(G) is the associated stack over M(1). For S = Spec k with k separably closed, G-structures on E/k are exactly the isomorphism classes of geometrically connected G-torsors on E°/k. If Z(G) = 1 the presheaf is already a sheaf. In general the map from torsors to G-structures need not be injective or surjective. M(G) → M(1) is finite étale, whereas Adm(G)‾ → M(1)‾ is typically not representable.
items.note: Following [Che18], with [DM69, §5] and [PdJ95] as antecedents. API: the sheaf T_G, its functoriality in G, the Aut(G)-action, and the induced stack over M(1). Tests: for G = ℤ/nℤ × ℤ/nℤ one recovers full level-n structures. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: The paper defines T_G for any finite group G (§2.5, p. 23), not only for 2-generated G. M(G) is empty unless G is 2-generated; 2-generation is assumed only in §2.5.3.

items.name: The fundamental properties of M(G) (Theorem 2.5.2)
items.statement: Let G be a finite group and f : M(G) → M(1) the forgetful map, over ℤ[1/|G|]. (1) M(G) is a Noetherian smooth separated Deligne–Mumford stack and f is finite étale. (2) M(G) has a coarse moduli scheme M(G), normal, affine and finite over M(1) ≅ Spec ℤ[1/|G|][j], smooth of relative dimension 1 over ℤ[1/|G|], and étale over the complement of j = 0, 1728. If 6 | |G| or S' is a regular Noetherian ℤ[1/|G|]-scheme, M(G) ×_{ℤ[1/|G|]} S' is the (normal) coarse scheme of M(G) ×_{ℤ[1/|G|]} S'. (3) For an elliptic curve E/S', a geometric point x̄ ∈ E° over s̄ ∈ S' and L the set of primes dividing |G|, the outer representation ρ_{E,x̄} : π₁(S',s̄) → Out(π₁^L(E°_s̄,x̄)) makes Epi^ext(π₁^L(E°_s̄,x̄),G) a finite π₁(S',s̄)-set. Its finite étale cover of S' is the pullback of M(G) along E/S', and T_G(E/S') is in bijection with the ρ-invariant elements. (4) For E over an algebraically closed field k with char k ∤ |G| and x₀ ∈ E°(k), taking monodromy gives f^{−1}(x_E) ≅ Epi^ext(π₁^ét(E°,x₀),G); over ℂ, f^{−1}(x_E) ≅ Epi^ext(Π,G) with Π := π₁^top(E°(ℂ),x₀). Hence M(G) = ∅ unless G is 2-generated. Put γ₀ : (a,b) ↦ (ab^{−1},a), γ₁₇₂₈ : (a,b) ↦ (b^{−1},a), γ_∞ : (a,b) ↦ (a,ab) and γ_{−I} : (a,b) ↦ (a^{−1},b^{−1}), and let f‾ : M(G)‾ → M(1)‾_ℂ be the map of smooth compactifications. Then f‾^{−1}(j(E)) ≅ Epi^ext(Π,G)/⟨γ_{−I}⟩ for j(E) ≠ 0, 1728, compatibly with the projection from f^{−1}(x_E); moreover f‾^{−1}(0) ≅ Epi^ext(Π,G)/⟨γ₀⟩, f‾^{−1}(1728) ≅ Epi^ext(Π,G)/⟨γ₁₇₂₈⟩ and f‾^{−1}(∞) ≅ Epi^ext(Π,G)/⟨γ_{−I},γ_∞⟩. (5) Π is free of rank 2 and Π^ab ≅ H₁(E,ℤ). With α : Out(Π) → GL(H₁(E,ℤ)) and Out⁺(Π) := α^{−1}(SL(H₁(E,ℤ))), α is an isomorphism (Nielsen) and the orientation-preserving mapping class group Γ_E of E°(ℂ) is identified with Out⁺(Π). So π₁^top(M(1)^an,E) ≅ Γ_E ≅ Out⁺(Π) ≅ SL₂(ℤ) and, by Riemann existence for stacks, π₁^ét(M(1)_ℚ‾,E) ≅ Out⁺(Π)^∧; the bijection f^{−1}(x_E) ≅ Epi^ext(Π,G) is Out⁺(Π)-equivariant. (6) On the category of finite 2-generated groups with surjections, G ↦ (M(G) → M(1)) is an epimorphism-preserving functor to stacks finite étale over M(1), sending f : G₁ ↠ G₂ to X° ↦ X°/ker f; on fibres it is post-composition f_* : Epi^ext(Π,G₁) → Epi^ext(Π,G₂). (7) (Cofinality: Asada with Belyi) every stack finite étale over M(1)_ℚ‾ is dominated by a connected component of some M(G)_ℚ‾. For every smooth projective curve X/ℚ‾ there are G, a component M_X ⊂ M(G)_ℚ‾ (a scheme) and a finite étale, even Galois, map M_X → X, with Galois action defined over the field of definition of M_X as an element of π₀(M(G)_ℚ‾).
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.5.1, pp. 24–27, Theorem 2.5.2, assembled from [Che18], [BBCL20] and [Asa01]
items.note: Part (5) uses a theorem of Nielsen that Out⁺(Π) ≅ SL₂(ℤ) acts on the free group as expected, and the Riemann existence theorem for stacks. Part (7) uses Asada's and Belyi's theorems. This is the bridge from geometry to combinatorics used throughout. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Parts (4)–(7) are misdescribed. (7) is cofinality (Asada's theorem with Belyi's), not 'the arithmetic action'. (4) contains the descriptions of the coarse fibres over j ≠ 0, 1728 and over j = 0, 1728, ∞ through γ₀, γ₁₇₂₈, γ_∞, γ_{−I}. These give deg(coarse component) = |O/⟨γ_{−I}⟩| and are used for Theorem 1.1.2, Theorem 4.10.5 and the cusp count in §5.6. The base-change clause of (2) is omitted.

items.name: Deformation theory of stable marked G-curves (Proposition 2.5.3)
items.statement: Let k be algebraically closed of characteristic coprime to |G| and x : Spec k → H‾_G a geometric point given by a stable marked G-curve (C/k,R) with image y = (C/G, R/G) in M(1)‾. On universal deformation rings the map H‾_G → M(1)‾ is given by Λ[[T]] → Λ[[t]], T ↦ t^e, where e = 1 if C is smooth and otherwise e is the order of the stabiliser of any node of C. In particular H‾_G → M(1)‾ is flat, H_G → M(1) is étale, and H_G ⊂ H‾_G and Adm⁰(G) ⊂ Adm(G)‾ are open and dense.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.5.2, pp. 27–28, Proposition 2.5.3, quoting [BR11, Theorem 5.1.5]
items.note: This is the source of the ramification index of the forgetful map at the cusps. Tests: a smooth cover gives e = 1; a cuspidal cover whose nodes have stabiliser of order e gives T ↦ t^e.

items.name: Two-generation is necessary (Corollary 2.5.4)
items.statement: If G cannot be generated by two elements then Adm(G)‾ is empty.
items.note: Because the monodromy of a connected G-cover of a once-punctured genus-1 surface is a surjection from a free group of rank 2. Tests: G = (ℤ/2)³ gives an empty stack. Review note on status: Its proof needs the prime-to-p fundamental group of E° in characteristics not dividing |G| (SGA1 X Cor. 3.10). That input is in the direction of InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.1 (tame quotients, specialization); see the coverage row.

items.name: Vertical automorphism groups (Definition 2.5.5)
items.statement: For a map of algebraic stacks f : X → Y and a T-point t, the vertical automorphism group of t is the kernel of f_* : Aut_{X(T)}(t) → Aut_{Y(T)}(f(t)); for Deligne–Mumford stacks f is representable exactly when all vertical automorphism groups of geometric points are trivial. Unless said otherwise the vertical automorphism group is taken relative to the map to M(1)‾ and written Aut^v(t); for a point of Adm⁰(G) given by π : C → E it is the group of G-equivariant automorphisms σ of C with π ∘ σ = π.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.5.2, p. 29, Definition 2.5.5 and the paragraph after it
items.note: API: the vertical group, its relation to representability, and its computation for covers. Tests: for a smooth cover it is Z(G) (Proposition 2.5.6).

items.name: Vertical automorphisms of smooth covers (Proposition 2.5.6)
items.statement: The vertical automorphism groups of geometric points of Adm⁰(G) are isomorphic to Z(G).
items.note: Proof route: such an automorphism restricts to an automorphism of the G-torsor over E_gen, hence is given by an element of G, and G-equivariance forces it to be central. Tests: G with trivial centre gives a representable map at smooth points.

items.name: Rigidification of a stack by a group of automorphisms (Theorem 2.5.7)
items.statement: Let H be a flat finitely presented separated group scheme over S and X an algebraic stack such that every object ξ carries a compatible embedding H(S) ↪ Aut_S(ξ). Then the rigidification X ⫽ H exists, together with a smooth surjective finitely presented map X → X ⫽ H, such that (a) H(S) lies in the kernel of Aut_S(ξ) → Aut_S(η); (b) X → X ⫽ H is a gerbe, universal for such maps; (c) over an algebraically closed field Aut(η) = Aut(ξ)/H; (d) coarse spaces agree and the map is a homeomorphism on topological spaces; (e) Deligne–Mumfordness is preserved and the map is étale; (f) smoothness and properness are preserved.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.5.2, pp. 29–30, Theorem 2.5.7, quoting [ACV03, Theorem 5.1.5]
items.note: Notation X ⫽ H follows [Rom0504]. The reviewed audit of AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry R09.5 records rigidification in the sense of auxiliary level structures, not this quotient-by-inertia construction, and neither is in the libraries. Review note on status: AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry:R09.5 ('Coarse spaces and rigidification') is the natural owner, but its description covers rigidification by auxiliary level, not the Abramovich–Corti–Vistoli rigidification X⫽H by a flat group of automorphisms. 'missing' is correct unless R09.5 is widened.

items.name: The compactified stack M(G)‾ and its comparison with Adm(G)‾ (Definition 2.5.9, Proposition 2.5.10)
items.statement: Set M(G)‾ := Adm(G)‾ ⫽ Z(G), with coarse space M(G)‾. Over S = Spec ℤ[1/|G|]: (a) Adm(G)‾ → M(G)‾ induces an isomorphism of coarse spaces Adm(G)‾ ≅ M(G)‾, hence a homeomorphism; both stacks are empty unless G is 2-generated. (b) The map φ : Adm⁰(G) → M(G) sending π : C → E to the G-structure of the torsor C_gen → E° is an étale gerbe and factors through an isomorphism Adm⁰(G) ⫽ Z(G) ≅ M(G), so M(G) is an open dense substack of M(G)‾. (c) M(G)‾ is smooth and proper of relative dimension 1 over S. (d) M(G)‾ → M(1)‾ is flat, proper and quasi-finite. (e) The coarse scheme M(G)‾, hence Adm(G)‾, is smooth and proper of relative dimension 1 over S. (f) A surjection f : G₁ ↠ G₂ of finite 2-generated groups induces, via C ↦ C/ker f, a proper, surjective, quasi-finite map M(f)‾ : M(G₁)‾ → M(G₂)‾ over M(1)‾, extending the map M(f) of Theorem 2.5.2(6).
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.5.2, pp. 30–31, Definition 2.5.9 and Proposition 2.5.10
items.note: Consequently the sets of connected components of Adm(G)‾, Adm⁰(G) and M(G) are in natural bijection, which is the fact used throughout to pass between geometry and combinatorics. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: In (f) the paper assumes f : G₁ ↠ G₂ is a surjection of finite 2-generated groups. Without it, surjectivity of M(f)‾ fails: if G₁ is not 2-generated then M(G₁)‾ = ∅ while M(G₂)‾ may be nonempty.

items.name: Cusps of M(G)‾ and noncongruence modular curves (Definition 2.5.11, Remark 2.5.12)
items.statement: A k-point of M(G)‾ (resp. M(G)‾, Adm(G)‾, Adm(G)‾) not lying in M(G) (resp. M(G), Adm⁰(G), Adm⁰(G)) is called a cusp or cuspidal object. The terminology is justified because the schemes M(G)‾_ℂ are disjoint unions of quotients of the upper half-plane by finite-index, possibly noncongruence, subgroups of SL₂(ℤ), whose cusps in the hyperbolic sense are exactly the points of M(G)‾_ℂ − M(G)_ℂ.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.5.2, p. 31, Definition 2.5.11 and Remark 2.5.12
items.note: Each component of M(G)_ℂ is thus a possibly noncongruence modular curve; §5.6 shows that for a density-one set of primes the components attached to SL₂(F_p) and trace −2 are noncongruence.

items.name: (G|A)-structures and absolute G-structures (Definition 2.5.13)
items.statement: Out(G) acts freely on the sheaf T_G of G-structures, so for a subgroup A ⊆ Out(G) the quotient T_G/A is again a finite locally constant sheaf; its sections are (G|A)-structures and the associated stack is M(G)/A. For A = Out(G) these are absolute G-structures and the stack is written M(G)^abs.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §2.5.3, p. 32, Definition 2.5.13 and the paragraph before it
items.note: Used for SL₂(F_q) with A = D(q), the group of diagonal outer automorphisms, which is what matches the GL₂(F_q)-conjugation on the character variety.

items.name: The Galois-theoretic dictionary (Situation 2.5.14)
items.statement: Let E/ℚ‾ be an elliptic curve, t ∈ E°(ℂ), Π := π₁^top(E°(ℂ),t) with a positively oriented basis a, b, and x_E the geometric point of M(1) given by E. The canonical injection Out⁺(Π) ↪ π₁(M(1)_ℚ‾,x_E) has dense image and identifies the profinite completion of Out⁺(Π) with π₁(M(1)_ℚ‾,x_E); for a finite 2-generated G the fibre of M(G) → M(1) over x_E is the set of geometrically connected G-torsors on E°, and taking monodromy gives an Out⁺(Π)-equivariant bijection α_{G,x_E} : f^{−1}(x_E) ≅ Epi^ext(Π,G) under which the Higman invariant becomes ϕ ↦ ϕ([b,a]). The fibre functor at x_E is an equivalence from finite étale stacks over M(1)_ℚ‾ to finite Out⁺(Π)-sets, compatible with the functor G ↦ M(G).
items.note: This 'Galois theoretic mantra' is invoked whenever a statement about components of M(G) is converted into one about Out⁺(Π)-orbits on Epi^ext(Π,G). Tests: the degree of a component over M(1) equals the size of the corresponding orbit, or twice it (Theorem 2.5.2).

items.name: Sheaf of relative differentials and relative dualizing sheaf for stacks
items.statement: For a representable morphism f : C → X of algebraic stacks, Ω_{C/X} is defined by descent from a smooth presentation, and for a representable flat proper finitely presented morphism with geometrically connected Cohen–Macaulay fibres the relative dualizing sheaf ω_{C/X} is defined by ω_{C/X}(t) := Γ(T, τ*ω_{C_T/T}) over schemes T → X, using that relative dualizing sheaves commute with arbitrary base change.
items.note: Relative dualizing complexes and Grothendieck duality are absent from both libraries; the stack-level definition is what §3 needs. API: base change, the descent construction, and the invertibility for prestable curves.

items.name: Very ampleness and the canonical map Ω → ω for marked curves (Lemma 3.1.3, Proposition 3.1.4)
items.statement: For a stable marked curve (f : C → X, R) over a scheme, ω_{C/X}(R)^{⊗3} is relatively very ample and f_*ω_{C/X}(R)^{⊗3} is locally free. For a prestable curve f : C → X of Noetherian algebraic stacks with a finite étale R ⊂ C making every base change a stable marked curve, there is a canonical map ϕ : Ω_{C/X} → ω_{C/X} which is an isomorphism at every geometric point where f is smooth.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §3.1.3, pp. 35–36, Lemma 3.1.3 and Proposition 3.1.4
items.note: Proof route: embed C in the projective bundle P(f*L) with L := f_*(ω_{C/X}(R)^{⊗3}) and use the theory of determinants [KM76]; for schemes this is Stacks 0E9Z. Tests: at a node the map is not an isomorphism; over the smooth locus it is.

items.name: The universal family and its reduced ramification divisor (Definition 3.2.1, Proposition 3.2.2)
items.statement: (Definition 3.2.1) The universal family C(G) → E(G) → Adm(G)‾ is representable, and its pullback along T → Adm(G)‾ is the cover C → E → T. The reduced ramification divisor R_{C(G)/E(G)} ⊂ C(G) is the closed substack of pairs (π,σ) with σ factoring through R_π. (Proposition 3.2.2) (a) Over S = Spec ℤ[1/|G|], let X ⊂ Adm(G)‾ be a connected component classifying covers with ramification index e ≥ 2, with universal family C → E → X. Then R_π is finite étale over X of degree |G|/e. For a geometric point z of R_π with stabiliser G_z, the connected components of R_π are all isomorphic, each Galois over X with Galois group isomorphic to a subgroup of N_G(G_z)/G_z. (b) Over S = Spec ℤ[1/|G|,ζ_e] the same holds, and the Galois groups are isomorphic to subgroups of C_G(G_z)/G_z.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §3.2, pp. 36–37, Definition 3.2.1 and Proposition 3.2.2
items.note: This bounds the obstruction d_X: d_X divides |C_G(⟨c⟩)/⟨c⟩| for a representative c of the Higman invariant. Tests: if G_z is self-centralising the divisor is totally split. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Needs e ≥ 2: for e = 1, R_π = ∅ has degree 0, not |G|/e (see the new issue on Propositions 2.2.6 and 3.2.2). Part (a) is over S = Spec ℤ[1/|G|]; the item states this only for the refined part.

items.name: Restriction of the dualizing sheaf to a ramified section (Lemma 3.3.1, Proposition 3.3.2)
items.statement: For a ring A, an A-flat ideal I and e ≥ 1, multiplication gives I^{⊗e} ≅ I^e and reduction gives I^{⊗e} ⊗_A A/I ≅ (I/I²)^{⊗e}. Consequently, for a connected component X ⊂ Adm(G)‾ with universal family C → E → X of ramification index e above the zero section σ_O, and a section σ : X → C over σ_O, there is a canonical isomorphism σ_O*ω_{E/X} ≅ (σ*ω_{C/X})^{⊗e}.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §3.3, pp. 37–38, Lemma 3.3.1 and Proposition 3.3.2
items.note: This is the geometric heart of the congruence: the pullback of the Hodge bundle along the forgetful map is an e-th tensor power. Tests: e = 1 gives an isomorphism of line bundles; the local model x = ξ^e.

items.name: Degrees of line bundles on 1-dimensional stacks (Lemma 3.4.1, Definition 3.4.2, Proposition 3.4.3)
items.statement: Let X be a connected proper algebraic stack of pure dimension 1 over a field k. If p_i : U_i → X (i = 1, 2) are finite flat surjections from connected schemes, then deg(p₁*L)/deg p₁ = deg(p₂*L)/deg p₂. So, when such a cover exists, deg(L) := deg(p*L)/deg p ∈ ℚ is well defined. Such a cover by a smooth k-scheme exists if X is a smooth separated generically tame 1-dimensional Deligne–Mumford stack of finite type over k whose coarse space is a scheme (quasi-projective, e.g. because X is proper) [KV04]. In particular it exists for Adm(G)‾_k and M(G)‾_k when char k ∤ 2|G|.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §3.4, pp. 38–39, Lemma 3.4.1, Definition 3.4.2 and Proposition 3.4.3, following [BDP17], [KV04], [EHKV01]
items.note: Degrees on a stack are rational, which is the second obstruction to the congruence. Tests: the degree of a line bundle pulled back from the coarse space is an integer divided by the generic automorphism order. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Proposition 3.4.3(a) as printed has no properness (or finite-type/quasi-projective) hypothesis, but its proof uses Theorem 2.1.9(f), which needs X proper (see the new issue). The item copies (a) unchanged; add 'proper' (true in both applications) or 'of finite type' (then the separated 1-dimensional coarse space is quasi-projective).

items.name: Local characters and integrality of degrees (Proposition 3.4.4, Definition 3.4.5, Propositions 3.4.6 and 3.4.7)
items.statement: For a locally finitely presented tame separated Deligne–Mumford stack with coarse scheme c : X → X, pullback along c is an equivalence from invertible sheaves on X to those invertible sheaves on X whose local characters at all geometric points are trivial, with quasi-inverse c_*. If X is connected tame smooth proper 1-dimensional with generic automorphism group of order n, then any invertible sheaf with trivial local characters satisfies deg(L) = (1/n) deg(c_*L) ∈ (1/n)ℤ. Moreover deg(f*L) = d · deg L for a finite flat map of degree d; deg(c*L) = deg(L)/n; and for f : Y → X inducing a finite flat map of coarse schemes, deg(f*L) = (n_X/n_Y) deg(f) deg(L).
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §3.4, pp. 39–41, Propositions 3.4.4, 3.4.6, 3.4.7, Definition 3.4.5, quoting [Ols12, Proposition 6.1]
items.note: The local character at a geometric point is the rank-1 representation of the automorphism group on the fibre. m_X is defined as the least m with (σ*Ω)^{⊗m} of trivial local character. Tests: on the stacky point Bμ_n a line bundle has degree in (1/n)ℤ.

items.name: The Hodge bundle has degree 1/24 (Proposition 3.4.8)
items.statement: Over ℚ‾, for the universal family E(1)‾ → M(1)‾ of 1-generalized elliptic curves with zero section σ_O, the Hodge bundle λ := σ_O*ω_{E(1)‾/M(1)‾} is an invertible sheaf on M(1)‾ of degree 1/24.
items.note: The factor 12 in the main congruence comes from here, through 12e/gcd(12e,md). Tests: λ^{⊗12} descends to O(1) on the coarse j-line; the discriminant Δ is a section of λ^{⊗12}. Review note on status: Inputs are planned elsewhere. AlgebraicModularFormsAndSerreWeights:R15.1 plans the Hodge bundle and the GAGA comparison with analytic forms; tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/ModularForms#10c--modular-forms-as-section-spaces-and-the-dimension-formulas plans dim M₁₂(SL₂(ℤ)) = 2. The stacky degree 1/24 itself is not planned, so 'missing' stands; the stage should cite them.

items.name: The main congruence (Theorem 3.5.1)
items.statement: Work over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0. Let X ⊂ Adm(G)‾ be a connected component with universal family C → E → X, reduced ramification divisor R_π and coarse scheme X. Let R ⊂ R_π be a connected component (this requires e ≥ 2) with coarse scheme R and induced map ε : R → X; then C' := C ×_X R → R has a section σ over the zero section of E' := E ×_X R. Put e := e_X, the ramification index above the zero section; d := d_X, the degree of the induced map of coarse schemes ε‾ : R → X; m := m_X, the least positive integer with (σ*Ω_{C'/R})^{⊗m} of trivial local characters. Then the induced map of coarse schemes f‾ : X → M(1)‾ ≅ P¹_j satisfies deg(f‾) ≡ 0 mod 12e/gcd(12e, md).
items.note: Proof route: base change to R so that a ramified section exists, apply Proposition 3.3.2 and Proposition 3.4.8, and use that degrees of line bundles on the coarse schemes are integers after clearing the denominators 12 and m and the degree d. Tests: for G = ℤ/2ℤ, Adm(ℤ/2ℤ) has e = 1 and degree 3 over M(1)‾, so the obstructions are necessary. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Omits the base: §3.5 works over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0 (p. 41). d must be the degree of the induced map of coarse schemes ε‾ : R → X; the stacky map ε has degree (n_X/n_R)·d. The item's 'deg(ε : R → X)' does not say which. (The item's C' := C ×_X R corrects the paper's misprint 'C ×_C R'.)

items.name: Vertical automorphism groups at smooth points (Proposition 3.5.2)
items.statement: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, let Y ⊂ Adm⁰(G) be a connected component classifying covers with Higman invariant 𝔠 ∋ c, and R a component of the reduced ramification divisor of the universal family over Y. Let r̄ be a geometric point of R over ȳ ∈ Y, corresponding to π : C → E and a point P ∈ π^{−1}(O). Then Aut^v(ȳ) = Z(G) and Aut^v(r̄) = Z(G) ∩ G_P = Z(G) ∩ ⟨c⟩ (G_P is conjugate to ⟨c⟩, and Z(G) ∩ ⟨c⟩ is conjugation-invariant).
items.note: Together with the cuspidal computation of §4.10 this controls m_X. Tests: for SL₂(F_q) with q odd and trace −2, Z(G) ∩ ⟨c⟩ = {±I} has order 2. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Minor: §3.5 works over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, where the Higman-invariant decomposition is defined.

items.name: Precuspidal and cuspidal G-curves and G-covers (Definitions 4.1.1–4.1.3)
items.statement: Throughout §4, k is an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 with a fixed compatible system {ζ_n}_{n≥1} of primitive n-th roots of unity (ζ_n^d = ζ_{n/d} for d | n). A precuspidal G-curve is a non-smooth prestable curve C over k with a faithful right G-action and a G-invariant divisor R ⊂ C finite étale over k such that C → C/G sends nodes to nodes and is étale on C_sm − R, and (C/G, R/G) is a nodal elliptic curve (a non-smooth 1-generalized elliptic curve). It is cuspidal if C is connected and the G-action is balanced at the nodes in the sense of Remark 2.1.5(d). Morphisms are G-equivariant maps preserving the divisors. A G-cover of a finite-type equidimension-1 scheme Y is a finite flat p : X → Y with a faithful right G-action on X such that p induces X/G ≅ Y. For a nodal elliptic curve (E,O), a precuspidal G-cover is a G-cover π : C → E such that (C, (C ×_E O)_red) is a precuspidal G-curve; equivalently π sends nodes to nodes and is étale on C_sm − π^{−1}(O). It is connected (resp. balanced) when C is connected (resp. the action is balanced at the nodes), and cuspidal when it is both. Morphisms are G-equivariant maps over E. C^{pc}_E ⊇ C^c_E denote the categories of precuspidal and cuspidal G-covers of E.
items.note: A precuspidal G-cover is an admissible G-cover exactly when it is cuspidal. Tests: a disconnected normalisation glued along a G-equivariant bijection; an unbalanced action is precuspidal but not cuspidal. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Omits the standing hypotheses of §4 (p. 43): everything is over Spec k with k an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 and a fixed compatible system {ζ_n} of primitive roots of unity (ζ_n^d = ζ_{n/d} for d | n). The same hypotheses govern items 55–71 and should be carried by them. Also omits the morphisms and what 'balanced' means (Remark 2.1.5(d)).

items.name: The boundary of Adm(G)‾ as a category of cuspidal covers (Proposition 4.1.4)
items.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, and let Adm^c(G) := Adm(G)‾ − Adm⁰(G) be the closed substack of non-smooth (cuspidal) objects. Sending a cuspidal G-curve (C,R) over k to the cuspidal G-cover C → C/G of the nodal elliptic curve (C/G, R/G) is an equivalence of categories {cuspidal G-curves} ≅ Adm^c(G)(k). For a nodal elliptic curve E over k, let Adm(G)‾_E be the fibre category over E ∈ M(1)‾, whose objects are admissible G-covers of E and whose morphisms induce the identity on E. Then C^c_E = Adm(G)‾_E. In particular the automorphism groups of objects of C^c_E are the vertical automorphism groups of the corresponding objects of Adm(G)‾.
items.note: This is what turns the computation of automorphism groups at the cusps into a combinatorial problem. Tests: the fibre of Adm(G)‾ over the nodal cubic. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Missing the standing hypothesis that k is algebraically closed of characteristic 0 (§4, p. 43). Adm^c(G)(k) and the fibre category are taken over such a k. Otherwise exact.

items.name: Tangential base points and the canonical generator of inertia (Definitions 4.2.1, 4.2.2)
items.statement: For a smooth curve X with a closed point x and X° := X − {x}, a tangential base point at x is a closed point t of the punctured tangent space T°_x; for a finite étale cover π : Y° → X° one writes Y°_t := π^{−1}(t) := F_{X°,t}(π) and π₁(X°,t) := Aut(F_{X°,t}). There is a canonical injection π₁(T°_x,t) ↪ π₁(X°,t), and, having fixed a compatible system {ζ_n}, the canonical generator of inertia γ_t ∈ π₁(T°_x,t) acts on the fibre of the n-th power cover of T°_x ≅ G_m by z ↦ ζ_n z.
items.note: NC.0 plans tangential base points for selected open curves, with the comparison of a rational and a tangential point on P¹ minus three points as its acceptance condition; its reviewed audit records that nothing of the kind exists in either library. The finer statements Chen needs are the next item.

items.name: Specialization to a ramified fibre (Proposition 4.2.3)
items.statement: Let X be a smooth curve over k (algebraically closed, characteristic 0), x ∈ X a closed point and X° := X − {x}. (a) There is a canonical isomorphism T*_xX ≅ T*_0T_x, functorial in (X,x). If t is a tangential base point at x, then on the n-th power cover T_x → T_x, z ↦ z^n (whose restriction to T°_x ≅ G_m is the connected degree-n cover), γ_t acts on the fibre over t by z ↦ ζ_n z, so the corresponding deck transformation multiplies the cotangent line at 0 of the source by ζ_n. (b) Let π : Y → X be a finite map of smooth curves, étale over X°. Then every connected component of Y_{(x)} has a unique point over 0 ∈ T_x, and π_{(x)}^{−1}(0) is canonically in bijection with Y_x := π^{−1}(x). Sending y ∈ Y_t to the unique point of Y_{(x)} over 0 in its component induces a canonical bijection ⟨γ_t⟩\Y_t ≅ π_{(x)}^{−1}(0) ≅ Y_x (specialization to the ramified fibre). This bijection is functorial in π, as an isomorphism of functors FEt_{X°} → Sets.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §4.2, pp. 45–46, Proposition 4.2.3 (p. 45), with the analytic counterpart in Remark 4.2.4 (p. 45) and the variant in Remark 4.2.5 (p. 46)
items.note: The specialization map ⟨γ_t⟩\Y_t ≅ Y_x is what lets the cusp analysis compare fibres at a tangential base point with fibres at the ramification points. Tests: for the n-th power map on G_m the inertia orbits are the points of the ramified fibre. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: The second clause of (a) copies a garbled sentence of the paper (see the new issue on Proposition 4.2.3): γ_t ∈ π₁(T°_x,t) does not act on T*_xX, and n is undefined. The meaningful statement concerns the n-th power cover of T_x, equivalently a point of ramification index n over x, which is how Proposition 4.4.3(a) uses it. The locator pages are wrong.

items.name: The fundamental groupoid of P¹ − {0,1,∞} and good symmetric paths (Definition 4.3.1)
items.statement: Let P* := P¹ − {0,1,∞} over k (algebraically closed, characteristic 0), with fundamental groupoid Π_{P*}. Its objects are the fibre functors F_x at geometric or tangential base points x, and its morphisms δ : x ⇝ y are isomorphisms F_x ≅ F_y. For γ ∈ π₁(P*,y), γ^δ := δ^{−1}γδ ∈ π₁(P*,x). Let ι : z ↦ 1/z, fix a tangential base point t₀ at 0 and put t_∞ := ι(t₀). Let γ₀, γ_∞, γ₁ be the canonical generators of inertia at t₀, t_∞ and at a tangential base point t₁ at 1. A path δ : t₀ ⇝ t_∞ is good if γ₀ and γ_∞^δ topologically generate π₁(P*,t₀) and γ_∞^δ γ₁^ε γ₀ = 1 for some path ε : t₀ ⇝ t₁. It is symmetric if ι_*δ = γ₀^r · δ^{−1} · γ_∞^s for some r, s ∈ ℤ. Symmetric good paths exist: by comparison with the topological theory over ℂ (Remark 4.2.4), take the path running along (0, 1−ε), turning counterclockwise around 1 and continuing along (1+ε, ∞). For a good path δ, Π := π₁(P*,t₀) is free profinite of rank 2 on γ₀ and γ_∞^δ.
items.note: Good paths exist by comparison with the topological theory over ℂ. The symmetry condition is what makes the δ-invariant behave predictably under the [−1]-pullback (Proposition 4.9.1). AnabelianGeometryAndNonabelianChabauty NC.0 plans the fundamental groupoid and tangential points but not this calculus of good symmetric paths. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: Omits the existence statement that the later results rely on: symmetric good paths exist (§4.3, p. 46, from the analytic theory of Remark 4.2.4). Proposition 4.9.1 and Theorem 4.10.3 assume a symmetric good path. Also r, s ∈ ℤ and t₁, γ₁ (tangential base point at 1 and its canonical generator of inertia) should be named.

items.name: The category C^≻_{P¹} of covers with a gluing datum (Definitions 4.4.1, 4.4.2, 4.4.6)
items.statement: C^≻_{P¹} is the category of pairs (q : D → P¹, α) where q is a possibly disconnected G-cover of P¹ branched only over 0, 1, ∞ and α is a G-equivariant bijection between the fibres over 0 and ∞. A standard normalization of a nodal elliptic curve E is a finite birational ν : P¹ → E identifying 0 and ∞ to the node and sending 1 to the origin. An object of C^≻_{P¹} is connected when the glued precuspidal G-curve is connected.
items.note: This is the normalisation picture of a cuspidal cover: normalising a cuspidal G-cover of a nodal elliptic curve gives a G-cover of P¹ branched over three points together with the gluing bijection of the fibres over the two preimages of the node.

items.name: Monodromy at the tangential fibres (Proposition 4.4.3)
items.statement: Let (q : D → P¹, α) ∈ C^≻_{P¹}, x₀ ∈ D_{t₀} and δ : t₀ ⇝ t_∞ a path. Let ϕ_x be the monodromy representation at x (γ·x = x·ϕ_x(γ)) and χ_y : G_y → GL(T*_yD) the local representation at y ∈ D₀ ⊔ D_∞. Then: (a) G_{[x₀]} = ⟨ϕ_{x₀}(γ₀)⟩ and χ_{[x₀]}(ϕ_{x₀}(γ₀)) = ζ_n with n := |G_{[x₀]}|. (b) G_{[δx₀]} = ⟨ϕ_{δx₀}(γ_∞)⟩ and χ_{[δx₀]}(ϕ_{δx₀}(γ_∞)) = ζ_n with n := |G_{[δx₀]}|. (c) ϕ_{δx₀}(γ) = ϕ_{x₀}(γ^δ) for all γ ∈ π₁(P*,t_∞). (d) ϕ_{δ^{−1}x_∞}(γ) = ϕ_{x_∞}(γ^{δ^{−1}}) for all γ ∈ π₁(P*,t₀) and x_∞ ∈ D_{t_∞}. (e) ϕ_{xg}(γ) = g^{−1}ϕ_x(γ)g for all g ∈ G, γ ∈ π₁(P*,q(x)) and every unramified or tangential base point x of D.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §4.4, p. 48, Proposition 4.4.3, with the structures (a)–(e) set up on pp. 47–48
items.note: Here ϕ_x is the monodromy representation at x and χ the character by which the stabiliser acts on the cotangent space at the specialised point. Tests: conjugating the base point conjugates the monodromy. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: (d) reproduces a misprinted quantifier (p. 48, new issue): it must be γ ∈ π₁(P*,t₀), since ϕ_{δ^{−1}x_∞} is defined on π₁(P*,t₀). n in (a) and (b) is the order of the stabiliser and should be stated. Locator page wrong.

items.name: Gluing along a G-equivariant bijection (Lemma 4.4.4, Theorem 4.4.5)
items.statement: Given (π : D → P¹, α) with |π^{−1}(0)| = n, the pushout D_α of D along the identification β given by α exists in schemes; ν : D → D_α is finite surjective, identifies the topological space of D_α with the quotient of D by α, has Γ(U,O_{D_α}) = {f : f(x) = f(α(x))}, makes D_α a prestable curve whose nodes are the images of π^{−1}({0,∞}), identifies D with a normalization of D_α, is an isomorphism away from π^{−1}({0,∞}), and the canonical map D_α → E₀ to the nodal elliptic curve obtained by gluing 0 to ∞ in P¹ (with origin the image of 1) is a precuspidal G-cover; this defines the gluing functor Glue : C^≻_{P¹} → C^{pc}_{E₀}. Conversely, for a nodal elliptic curve E and a standard normalization ν, the categories C^{pc}_E and C^≻_{P¹} are groupoids and Ξ_ν : C^{pc}_E → C^≻_{P¹} is an equivalence, with quasi-inverse the gluing functor.
items.note: Tests: the degree-1 cover P¹ → P¹ glues to the nodal cubic; the number of irreducible components of the glued curve equals the number of components of D.

items.name: Balanced objects of C^≻_{P¹} (Lemma 4.5.1, Proposition 4.5.2, Definition 4.5.3)
items.statement: For (q,α) in C^≻_{P¹}, x₀ ∈ D_{t₀} and a path δ : t₀ ⇝ t_∞, α([x₀]) = [δx₀·h] for some h ∈ G, unique modulo the coset H_{δ,x₀} := G_{[δx₀]}h. (Lemma 4.5.1) For another path δ′ : t₀ ⇝ t_∞ and h ∈ H_{δ,x₀}, [δ′x₀·ϕ_{x₀}(δ′^{−1}δ)h] = [δx₀·h], i.e. ϕ_{x₀}(δ′^{−1}δ)h ∈ H_{δ′,x₀}. (Proposition 4.5.2) The following are equivalent: (a) for some (equivalently any) x₀ ∈ D_{t₀}, x_∞ ∈ D_{t_∞} with [x_∞] = α([x₀]), ϕ_{x₀}(γ₀)^{−1} = ϕ_{x_∞}(γ_∞); (b) for some (equivalently any) x₀, δ and h ∈ H_{δ,x₀}, ϕ_{x₀}(γ₀)^{−1} = h^{−1}ϕ_{x₀}(γ_∞^δ)h. A precuspidal G-cover p is balanced if and only if Ξ(p) satisfies these conditions. (Definition 4.5.3) Such objects of C^≻_{P¹} are called balanced.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §4.5, pp. 50–51, Lemma 4.5.1, Proposition 4.5.2 and Definition 4.5.3
items.note: Balancedness is the local condition at the nodes expressed through monodromy; it is the combinatorial shadow of condition (6) of Definition 2.1.4. Review (REV-PAPER-CHEN-24): statement corrected against the paper: The locator cites Lemma 4.5.1, but the statement does not state it. The lemma is never used later in the paper; either state it (below) or drop it from the locator.

items.name: Galois correspondence for precuspidal G-covers (Definition 4.6.1, Proposition 4.6.2)
items.statement: For a good path δ, Sets^{(Π,G)_δ,≻} is the category of pairs (F,α) where F is a finite set with a left Π-action commuting with a free transitive right G-action and α : ⟨γ₀⟩\F → ⟨γ_∞^δ⟩\F is a G-equivariant bijection, called a precuspidal G-datum. The functor F^≻_δ : C^≻_{P¹} → Sets^{(Π,G)_δ,≻} sending (q,α) to (D_{t₀}, F^≻_δ(α)) is an equivalence of categories.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §4.6, pp. 51–52, Definition 4.6.1 and Proposition 4.6.2
items.note: Here Π := π₁(P*,t₀). This is the passage from geometry to pure combinatorics for the cusps; it uses the Galois theory of P¹ minus three points and the specialization maps of Proposition 4.2.3. Review note on status: Stays missing. tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/BelyiMaps#layer-4-triangle-groups (4.2) classifies connected three-point covers combinatorially by permutation representations of triangle groups. That is only a partial supplier for the Galois correspondence behind Proposition 4.6.2: it has no tangential base points and no gluing data.

items.name: Graphs of components and combinatorial connectedness (Definitions 4.7.1, 4.7.2, 4.7.5, Propositions 4.7.3, 4.7.4, 4.7.6)
items.statement: A precuspidal G-datum is balanced when ϕ_x(γ₀)^{−1} = h^{−1}ϕ_x(γ_∞^δ)h for some, equivalently any, x and h ∈ H_{δ,x}. Following Bass, a graph is (V,E,σ,τ) with a fixed-point-free involution τ on edges; the graph Γ_π of a precuspidal G-cover has vertices the components of the normalisation and edges the points over 0 and ∞, and C is connected exactly when Γ_π is. The graph Γ_{F,α} of a precuspidal G-datum has vertices Π\F and edges ⟨γ₀⟩\F ⊔ ⟨γ_∞^δ⟩\F, is isomorphic to Γ_π under the equivalences, and is connected exactly when, for some (equivalently any) x ∈ F, G is generated by the monodromy group M_x := ϕ_x(Π) together with H_{δ,x}, equivalently with any single h ∈ H_{δ,x}. A datum is cuspidal when connected and balanced, and the equivalences Ξ and F^≻_δ restrict to the connected, the balanced and the cuspidal objects.
items.note: Tests: a datum with M_x = G is automatically connected; the graph of a disconnected cover has as many components as the cover.

items.name: Cuspidal data and the δ-invariant (Proposition 4.8.1, Definitions 4.8.2–4.8.3, Theorem 4.8.4, Definition 4.8.5)
items.statement: A precuspidal G-datum (F,α) (relative to a good path δ) is cuspidal if and only if, for some (equivalently any) x ∈ F and h ∈ H_{δ,x}: (a) ϕ_x(γ_∞^δ) = hϕ_x(γ₀)^{−1}h^{−1}, and (b) G = ⟨h, ϕ_x(γ₀)⟩. Let G act on G×G by simultaneous conjugation and ℤ act on the right by (u,h)·k = (u, u^k h). These actions commute and preserve generating pairs. Put I(G) := G\{(u,h) ∈ G×G : ⟨u,h⟩ = G}/ℤ and write [[u,h]] ∈ I(G) for the class of a generating pair. For a generating pair (u,h), let (F_{u,h}, α_{u,h}) be the datum on the right G-torsor G with γ_∞^δ·x = ux, γ₀·x = h^{−1}u^{−1}hx and α_{u,h}(⟨γ₀⟩x) = ⟨γ_∞^δ⟩hx. It is cuspidal, with monodromy group M_{u,h} := ⟨u, h^{−1}u^{−1}h⟩ at 1_G. Put Inv_δ(F,α) := [[ϕ_x(γ_∞^δ), h]] ∈ G\(G×G)/ℤ. It is independent of x ∈ F and h ∈ H_{δ,x} and lies in I(G) for cuspidal data. It induces a bijection from isomorphism classes of cuspidal data onto I(G), with inverse (u,h) ↦ (F_{u,h}, α_{u,h}). Via Ξ and F^≻_δ this gives a bijection π₀(Adm(G)‾_E) ≅ I(G) for a nodal elliptic curve E over k.
items.locator: arXiv:2011.12940v2 (19 June 2021), §4.8, pp. 55–57, Proposition 4.8.1, Definitions 4.8.2, 4.8.3, 4.8.5 and Theorem 4.8.4
